section.title: Chapter review and discovery problems
section.p: This chapter began with a simple observation:
section.md: f'(x)\gt 0 \text{ means rising}, \qquad f'(x)\lt 0 \text{ means falling}.
section.p: That observation grew into a much larger picture. The derivative gives more than instantaneous rate. It gives shape, turning, bending, bounds, and sometimes limits.

subsection.title: Proof practice with the Mean Value Theorem

paragraphs.title: A function with positive derivative is increasing
paragraphs.p: Suppose f is continuous on an interval I, differentiable at the interior points of I, and f'(x)\gt 0 throughout the interior of I. Use the Mean Value Theorem to prove that f is increasing on I.

paragraphs.title: A zero derivative forces a constant function
paragraphs.p: Suppose f'(x)=0 for every x in an interval I. Use the Mean Value Theorem to prove that f is constant on I.

paragraphs.title: Equal derivatives differ by a constant
paragraphs.p: Suppose f'(x)=g'(x) for every x in an interval I. Prove that f(x)-g(x) is constant on I.

paragraphs.title: How many roots can a derivative control?
paragraphs.p: Suppose f is differentiable on an interval and f'(x)\gt 0 throughout the interval. Prove that f(x)=0 has at most one solution.

paragraphs.title: Two zeros force a zero derivative
paragraphs.p: Suppose f is continuous on [a,b], differentiable on (a,b), and f(a)=f(b)=0. Prove that there is some c\in(a,b) such that f'(c)=0. Then explain why this is exactly Rolle's Theorem in a special case.

paragraphs.title: Three zeros force a zero second derivative
paragraphs.p: Suppose f is continuous on [a,b], differentiable on (a,b), and has three zeros in the interval. Assume f'' exists where needed. Prove that there is some point c where f''(c)=0.
Hint: apply Rolle's Theorem more than once.

paragraphs.p: Use the previous problem to explain why a quadratic polynomial cannot have three distinct real roots unless it is the zero polynomial.

paragraphs.p: Pick a smooth function f and two points a\lt b. Draw the secant line through (a,f(a)) and (b,f(b)). Find a point c where the tangent is parallel to that secant. Then verify your picture algebraically.

paragraphs.p: Find a function f such that f'(0)=0, but 0 is not a local maximum or local minimum. Explain why your example has a horizontal tangent without a turning point.

subsection.title: Where this points
subsection.p: This chapter taught us how to read a graph from its derivatives. That is already useful: we can locate peaks, valleys, flat points, bends, and asymptotes.
But many real questions do not start by asking for a graph. They ask for a choice.
What shape gives the largest volume?
What route takes the least time?
What price gives the greatest profit?
How fast is one quantity changing when another quantity is changing?
Those questions still use derivatives, but now the graph is only part of the story. The next chapter turns shape information into decisions: related rates, optimization, and models.
